content.title: About
content.content: Blackberries are the edible berries of the Rubus fruticosus shrub, native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. The fruits are dark purple to black, sweet‑tart in flavor, and have a soft, slightly fibrous texture. Blackberries are eaten fresh and are also used in baking, desserts, jams, and juices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blackberries belong to the rose family and are closely related to raspberries and currants.
High anthocyanin content gives the berries their deep color and strong antioxidant properties.
Wild varieties can be more tart than cultivated ones.
Traditional medicine uses blackberries to aid digestion and reduce inflammation.
Blackberries ripen from late summer through early autumn.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The berries provide vitamin C, anthocyanins, and polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber in blackberries promotes regular bowel movements and may reduce constipation risk.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other phytochemicals enhance the body’s immune defenses.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Flavonoids can improve insulin sensitivity and aid in glucose control.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and dietary fiber contribute to healthy blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to blackberries.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If not organic, berries should be washed thoroughly to remove any chemical residues.

items.title: Gastrointestinal discomfort
items.content: Consuming large amounts may cause gas due to the high fiber content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blackberries can be eaten fresh, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, salads, baked into pies, jams, and sauces. For a softer texture, gently mash the berries or strain them through a sieve.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh blackberries in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze the berries in a single layer on a tray, then transfer to a freezer bag – they keep well for up to 12 months.

green-beans-fresh-cooked-with-oil.title: Green beans, fresh, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Green beans are young pods of legume plants harvested before the seeds fully develop. When cooked with a small amount of oil, they retain a crisp texture and mild flavor while enhancing the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green beans belong to the legume family and are closely related to peas, lentils, and soy.
They are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and carotenoids, supporting immune health.
Traditional cuisines worldwide steam, sauté, or braise them with aromatic herbs.
Their fiber content helps regulate blood sugar levels.
When stored properly, fresh pods can stay crisp for up to a week in the refrigerator.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Green beans provide vitamin B6, folate, and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of fresh beans contains about 2 g of protein, making it a valuable addition to vegetarian meals.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety, and helps maintain normal cholesterol levels.

items.title: Abundant antioxidants
items.content: Vitamin C, carotenoids, and flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and magnesium in green beans contribute to strong bones.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Beans contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

items.title: Potential food toxins
items.content: Raw or undercooked pods may contain phytohemagglutinin, a compound that can cause gastrointestinal upset; cooking neutralizes it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Quickly sauté the beans in olive or sunflower oil with garlic and spices, or add them to salads, soups, and stews. For a softer texture, blanch for 3–5 minutes before a brief stir‑fry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh pods in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container to retain moisture. They stay crisp for 5–7 days. Freeze in portioned bags for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled, ready-to-heat potato is pre‑cooked potato packaged in single‑serve portions. It retains its natural flavor and texture, and after a quick microwave or stovetop reheating it is ready to eat within minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is one of the world’s most consumed vegetables, grown in over 100 countries.
Boiled potatoes retain a high amount of vitamin C when not over‑cooked.
Ready‑to‑heat potatoes are popular in cafeterias, office canteens and as a quick side dish at home.
When stored properly (refrigerated up to 5 days) the product stays fresh and tasty.
Potatoes contain resistant starch, which can support a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slowly digestible carbs that give lasting satiety.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Boiled potatoes keep vitamin C, an antioxidant that supports the immune system.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Potatoes contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potato.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added to the package, monitor sodium intake, especially for those with hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial growth if improperly stored
items.content: Storing above 4 °C for more than 5 days can allow bacterial proliferation.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should control portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or on the stovetop, then add butter, herbs or spices to taste. It works well as a side for meat, fish, or in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C, up to 5 days after opening. Do not freeze. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry juice 100 % is a completely natural beverage made from ripe fresh strawberries without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright aroma, sweet‑tart taste and retains most of the vitamins and antioxidants characteristic of fresh berries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberries are one of the most popular berry flavors worldwide, and their aroma is widely used in cuisine and perfumery.
Strawberry juice retains a large portion of vitamin C, which is lost during heat processing.
Strawberry juice is often used in baby foods because of its mild taste and high nutritional value.
In Russia, strawberry juice is traditionally served in the summer, but frozen berries make it available year‑round.
Strawberry juice can serve as a base for cocktails, smoothies and dessert sauces.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins in strawberry juice help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium in the juice contributes to normal blood pressure, and polyphenols may improve vascular function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: A small amount of soluble fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low‑calorie beverage
items.content: Without added sugar, strawberry juice is relatively low in calories, making it a good choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Strawberry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries, ranging from skin rashes to gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Even without added sugar, the natural sugars in the juice can be significant for people monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic nature of the juice may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Pasteurization
items.content: Heat treatment can degrade some vitamins; choose juice that undergoes minimal processing.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberry juice can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, used in smoothies, cocktails, dessert sauces, or as a base for fruit punches. It can also be diluted with water or sweetened with honey for a milder flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days. Frozen juice retains quality for up to 6 months.

turkey-light-meat-roasted-skin-eaten.title: Turkey, light meat, roasted, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. Light turkey meat roasted with the skin on has a mild flavor, moderately dry texture, and a subtle aroma. The skin, cooked until crisp, is edible and adds extra flavor and healthy fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
Light turkey meat contains less fat than dark meat, but the skin retains some beneficial fats.
Roasting with the skin helps retain moisture, keeping the meat juicier.
In the United States, turkey is strongly associated with Thanksgiving.
Edible turkey skin is rich in collagen, which is beneficial for skin and joints.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Light turkey meat is an excellent source of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, turkey contains less saturated fat, making it a heart‑friendlier option.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey provides niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies selenium, zinc, and phosphorus, important for immunity, bone health, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: Crispy turkey skin contains collagen that may help maintain skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat or skin.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Roasting often involves added salt; excess sodium can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Possible bacteria
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; ensure it reaches an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: Cholesterol in the skin
items.content: The skin is higher in cholesterol; those with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sliced roasted turkey with skin can be served as a main dish, added to salads, sandwiches, or incorporated into hot meals. The crisp skin can be eaten as a snack, seasoned with herbs or spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑grade bag for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.
